leadership-v06-the-four-golden-signals.essentialQuestion: For a checkout API over one minute — 12,000 requests, 180 failures, a 99th-percentile latency of 850 ms against a 500 ms target, and a worker pool 92% busy — which golden signal shows users are affected now, and which predicts the next problem?
leadership-v06-the-four-golden-signals.verifiedBoundary: Google SRE identifies latency, traffic, errors, and saturation as four particularly useful signals for monitoring user-facing systems.
leadership-v06-the-four-golden-signals.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: one minute of measurements for an invented checkout API. The SRE book's four golden signals are latency (the time to service a request), traffic (the demand on the system), errors (the rate of failed requests) and saturation (how full the service is).

Derivation: traffic is 12,000 / 60 = 200 requests per second; errors are 180 / 12,000 = 1.5% of requests; latency at the 99th percentile is 850 ms, 350 ms over the 500 ms target; saturation is 92% of worker capacity.

Independent check: 12,000 − 180 = 11,820 requests succeeded, and 11,820 / 12,000 = 98.5%, consistent with a 1.5% error rate. Latency and errors describe what users experience now; saturation describes how close the service is to running out of capacity.

Misconception to reject: 'a busy worker pool is the outage.' High saturation is a warning, not user impact by itself; the SRE book's monitoring philosophy pages primarily on symptoms that users experience, such as the latency and error rates here.

Change one factor: double the traffic to 400 requests per second with the same capacity. The pool would need 92% × 2 = 184% of its capacity, so work queues, latency rises further and errors follow. Saturation was the signal that predicted this.

Source and limits: the four golden signals are defined in chapter 6 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, 'Monitoring Distributed Systems': https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/. One minute of data is a snapshot; percentiles and error rates should be read over windows that match the objective.

leadership-v06-symptom-based-alerting.essentialQuestion: With a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, why does an error rate of 1.44% for one hour justify paging someone while a CPU alert at 80% often does not, and how is that threshold derived?
leadership-v06-symptom-based-alerting.verifiedBoundary: SRE monitoring guidance favors alerts tied to user-visible symptoms and actionable conditions rather than every internal metric change.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: a request-based SLO of 99.9% over 30 days (720 hours), so the error budget is 0.1% of requests in the window. Burn rate is how fast, relative to the SLO, the service consumes that budget. Traffic is assumed to be steady across the window.

Derivation: an error rate of 1.44% is 1.44 / 0.1 = 14.4 times the rate the SLO allows. One hour at burn rate 14.4 consumes 14.4 × 1 / 720 = 2% of the 30-day budget, the Site Reliability Workbook's recommended threshold for a page.
Independent check: at burn rate 14.4 the whole 30-day budget would be gone in 720 / 14.4 = 50 hours, about two days, which is fast enough that a person should act now.

Misconception to reject: 'alert on every likely cause.' A CPU alert at 80% can fire on a busy but healthy service and can stay silent during an outage caused by something else. The SRE book asks monitoring to answer what is broken and why, pages primarily on symptoms, and holds that every page should be actionable.

Change one factor: a smaller degradation of 0.6% errors for 6 hours is a burn rate of 6 and consumes 6 × 6 / 720 = 5% of the budget, the workbook's second paging threshold; at burn rate 1 over 3 days the workbook recommends a ticket instead of a page.

Source and limits: burn rate and the starting thresholds (2% in 1 hour at 14.4, 5% in 6 hours at 6, 10% in 3 days at 1) come from chapter 5 of The Site Reliability Workbook, 'Alerting on SLOs', https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/; the symptom-first principle is in chapter 6 of the SRE book, https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/. Thresholds should be tuned to each service's traffic and objective.

leadership-v06-toil.essentialQuestion: If every new service adds two manual certificate renewals a month at 20 minutes each, how does that work grow from 30 services to 60, and which properties make it toil rather than engineering?

leadership-v06-toil.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: each service needs two certificate renewals a month, each done by hand in 20 minutes. The team runs 30 services today and expects 60 within a year. The figures are invented.

Derivation: at 30 services the renewals take 30 × 2 × 20 = 1,200 minutes, 20 hours a month. At 60 services they take 2,400 minutes, 40 hours a month. The work doubles with the number of services: it scales linearly as the service grows.
Independent check: the work per service stays at 2 × 20 = 40 minutes a month, so the total is 40 minutes times the number of services, which gives 20 hours at 30 services and 40 hours at 60.

Misconception to reject: 'operational work that someone has to do is toil by definition.' The renewal is toil because it is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical and has no enduring value; a capacity design that prevents future outages is operational in subject but has enduring value, so it is not toil.

Change one factor: automate renewal with a one-time investment of 16 hours. At 60 services that removes 40 hours a month, so the automation pays for itself within the first month, and the saving keeps growing as services are added.

Source and limits: chapter 5 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, 'Eliminating Toil', defines toil by these properties, including that it scales linearly as a service grows: https://sre.google/sre-book/eliminating-toil/. Real renewal times vary, and automation needs its own maintenance.

leadership-v06-toil-reduction.essentialQuestion: With 40 engineering hours available this quarter and three toil sources to address, which work should come first, and why can fixing a cause beat automating its symptom?
leadership-v06-toil-reduction.verifiedBoundary: Reducing toil means automating, eliminating, or redesigning repetitive operational work so engineering time can shift toward durable improvements.
leadership-v06-toil-reduction.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Reducing toil means automating, eliminating, or redesigning repetitive operational work so engineering time can shift toward durable improvements.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use the evidence link to verify the definition of toil reduction, then identify one place the concept appears in a real system or problem. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: three invented toil sources: manual certificate renewals (20 hours a month; automation costs 16 hours), access requests (10 hours a month; automation costs 30 hours) and restarting a job that leaks memory (6 hours a month; fixing the leak costs 24 hours and removes the restarts entirely). The quarter offers 40 engineering hours.

Derivation: payback time is the one-time cost divided by the monthly saving: 16 / 20 = 0.8 months for renewals, 30 / 10 = 3 months for access requests and 24 / 6 = 4 months for the leak fix. Renewals come first. Renewals plus the leak fix cost 16 + 24 = 40 hours and save 26 hours a month; renewals plus access requests would cost 46 hours, which does not fit.
Independent check: over the remaining two months of the quarter, renewals plus the leak fix save 2 × 26 = 52 hours for a 40-hour investment, while renewals alone save 2 × 20 = 40 hours for 16 hours.
Misconception to reject: 'automate every manual task.' Automating the restarts would keep the leak and add a restart system to maintain; fixing the leak removes the work and its cause.
Change one factor: if access requests grow to 25 hours a month, their payback falls to 30 / 25 = 1.2 months, and the ranking changes. Re-rank toil sources whenever their volumes change.

Source and limits: chapter 5 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, 'Eliminating Toil', sets the goal of keeping toil below 50% of each SRE's time and describes engineering work that reduces future toil: https://sre.google/sre-book/eliminating-toil/. Payback ignores the maintenance cost of the new automation.

leadership-v06-on-call-readiness.essentialQuestion: How many engineers does a single-site team need to staff 24/7 on-call with a primary and a secondary under the SRE book's 25% on-call limit, and what does a shift with three incidents in 12 hours tell you?
leadership-v06-on-call-readiness.verifiedBoundary: An on-call system needs actionable alerts, clear escalation paths, access to operational context, and the authority to mitigate incidents.
leadership-v06-on-call-readiness.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use the evidence link to verify the definition of on-call readiness, then identify one place the concept appears in a real system or problem. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: a single-site team covers on-call around the clock with two people on call at all times (primary and secondary), and each engineer may spend at most 25% of their time on call. Incidents are counted per 12-hour shift. The team details are invented.
Derivation: two people must always be on call, and each can cover at most a quarter of the time, so the rotation needs at least 2 / 0.25 = 8 engineers.
Independent check: with 8 engineers and week-long shifts, each engineer is primary or secondary for 2 of every 8 weeks, which is 25% of their time.

Misconception to reject: 'more incidents per shift just means a busy week.' The SRE book reports that an incident takes about 6 hours on average once root-cause analysis, remediation and follow-up are included, which makes 2 incidents per 12-hour shift the practical maximum. Three incidents imply about 18 hours of work in a 12-hour shift, so follow-up work is being dropped.

Change one factor: if two engineers leave and six remain, each must be on call 2 / 6 ≈ 33% of the time, above the 25% limit. The book suggests a minimum of six engineers at each site for a dual-site team.

Source and limits: chapter 11 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, 'Being On-Call', describes the 25% on-call limit, the 6-hour average incident cost, the maximum of 2 incidents per 12-hour shift and the dual-site minimum of six per site: https://sre.google/sre-book/being-on-call/. These are Google's operating figures, not universal laws.

leadership-v06-runbook-purpose.essentialQuestion: Why does a tested runbook for a database failover shorten recovery, and how can you tell when a runbook has gone stale?
leadership-v06-runbook-purpose.verifiedBoundary: A runbook captures repeatable operational procedures and decision guidance so responders can execute known actions consistently.
leadership-v06-runbook-purpose.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented service fails over its primary database a few times a year. Without a runbook, responders reconstruct the steps during the incident; with one, they follow steps written and rehearsed in advance.

Derivation: the SRE book reports that recording best practices ahead of time in a playbook produced roughly a 3x improvement in mean time to repair compared with improvising. Applied to this example, a failover that takes 90 minutes when improvised would take about 30 minutes with a runbook, if the same improvement held.

Independent check: the runbook's last test was 9 months ago, and since then the database version, the replication topology and the DNS provider have changed, a total of 3 changes that touch failover. Each untested change is a step that may no longer work, so the runbook should be treated as unverified.
Misconception to reject: 'a runbook is documentation, so writing it once is enough.' A runbook is a procedure; its value depends on being correct for the current system, which only a test can show.
Change one factor: schedule a failover drill after every change that touches the failover path and at least quarterly. A drill that finds a broken step turns a slow incident into a scheduled fix.

Source and limits: chapter 1 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book reports that recording best practices in a playbook produces roughly a 3x improvement in MTTR compared with 'winging it': https://sre.google/sre-book/introduction/. That figure is Google's experience; the 90- and 30-minute values here are illustrative.

vocabulary.definition: Google SRE defines toil as operational work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, and lacking enduring value, especially when it scales linearly with service growth.
Toil reduction begins by identifying repetitive, manual, automatable work and then measuring whether changes actually reduce the recurring operational burden.
SRE distinguishes engineering work from toil partly by whether the work produces enduring improvements instead of repeated manual effort.
Reducing toil means automating, eliminating, or redesigning repetitive operational work so engineering time can shift toward durable improvements.
